metadata.title: LOS DEBERES ESCOLARES. UN ANÁLISIS SISTEMATIZADO CON ESPECIAL REFERENCIA AL CASO ESPAÑOL

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This article is a systematic analysis/review of the homework debate and does not conduct an original student-level large-scale assessment analysis. Although it references international datasets such as PISA and TIMSS (e.g., to describe cross-national patterns of homework time and related outcomes), it does not report an analytic sample, scaling/score estimation procedure, or the application of complex survey weights. Therefore, no ILSA student weight variables (e.g., TOTWGT/W_FSTUWT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are specified for estimation. Any weighting guidance that would normally apply to PISA/TIMSS microdata is not operationalized here because the paper does not fit models to microdata.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: Plausible Values (PVs) are not applicable because the paper does not estimate cognitive achievement outcomes from ILSA microdata; it synthesizes prior research and secondary reports. The paper discusses relationships and patterns (e.g., homework time and achievement) at a conceptual and descriptive level rather than fitting PV-based models on student responses. Missing-data handling is therefore not part of an original empirical estimation pipeline in this article.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: No original ILSA microdata sample is constructed. The paper synthesizes findings from prior meta-analyses and secondary analyses, and it references PISA and TIMSS results descriptively (e.g., cross-national comparisons of homework time) without defining an analytic subsample or inclusion/exclusion criteria for student records.

data.outcome_summary: This paper provides a systematic, narrative analysis of the homework debate with special reference to Spain, drawing on prior meta-analyses (e.g., Cooper) and on descriptive evidence from international large-scale assessments such as PISA and TIMSS. It does not run an original machine-learning or predictive modeling study on ILSA microdata; instead, it summarizes reported patterns: a moderate association between homework and school outcomes in secondary education, little to no association in primary education, and potential counterproductive effects when homework time exceeds roughly two hours per day. For Spain, it reports that students spend relatively more time on homework than in many other countries, while achievement is not necessarily higher. Methodologically, the paper emphasizes the correlational nature of much of the evidence and highlights limitations such as confounding (e.g., prior achievement, school quality) and the difficulty of isolating homework effects from other factors.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This record is not an empirical ML study and does not report an analytic dataset, student-level sample size, per-country counts, PV handling, missing-data strategy, or fitted predictive models. The absence of main findings rows and confounder/predictor extraction is consistent with the paper’s role as a systematic narrative analysis rather than a model-estimation paper. Consequently, fields that would normally be populated for ILSA-based predictive modeling (e.g., PV handling, missing-data handling, ML algorithms, performance metrics) are intentionally left empty or set to framework-appropriate defaults.
